symbols.name: Accessibility relation
symbols.summary: World v is accessible from world w in a Kripke frame.
symbols.body: World v is accessible from world w in a Kripke frame. Properties of R determine which modal principles hold. Together these facts witness ◇P at w in ordinary Kripke semantics.

examples.note: Together these facts witness ◇P at w in ordinary Kripke semantics.

limitations: Properties of R determine which modal principles hold.

symbols.name: Always operator
symbols.summary: φ holds at all relevant future times.
symbols.body: φ holds at all relevant future times. Whether the present is included depends on the temporal semantics. No relevant future state contains an error under the selected temporal semantics.

examples.note: No relevant future state contains an error under the selected temporal semantics.

limitations: Whether the present is included depends on the temporal semantics.

symbols.name: Because marker
symbols.summary: Introduces a stated reason.
symbols.body: Introduces a stated reason. An argument-layout convention, not normally an object-language connective. The marker introduces the stated supporting reasons.

examples.note: The marker introduces the stated supporting reasons.

limitations: An argument-layout convention, not normally an object-language connective.

symbols.name: Belief operator
symbols.summary: Agent a believes φ.
symbols.body: Agent a believes φ. Belief does not normally entail truth. A model can represent agent a believing P while P is false.

examples.note: A model can represent agent a believing P while P is false.

limitations: Belief does not normally entail truth.

symbols.name: Bounded existential quantifier
symbols.summary: Some member of A satisfies P.
symbols.body: Some member of A satisfies P. Notice conjunction here, compared with the conditional in bounded universal quantification. Expand as ∃x(x ∈ Students ∧ Passed(x)); the witness must actually be a student.

examples.note: Expand as ∃x(x ∈ Students ∧ Passed(x)); the witness must actually be a student.

limitations: Notice conjunction here, compared with the conditional in bounded universal quantification.

symbols.name: Bounded universal quantifier
symbols.summary: Every member of A satisfies P.
symbols.body: Every member of A satisfies P. A set-theoretic abbreviation rather than an additional core FOL quantifier. Expand as ∀x(x ∈ Students → Passed(x)); nonstudents need not pass.

examples.note: Expand as ∀x(x ∈ Students → Passed(x)); nonstudents need not pass.

limitations: A set-theoretic abbreviation rather than an additional core FOL quantifier.

symbols.name: Conjunction
symbols.summary: Both p and q are true.
symbols.body: Both p and q are true. Juxtaposition and multiplication signs are also used in Boolean algebra. Both the open door and the illuminated light are required.

examples.text: P means the door is open; Q means the light is on. P ∧ Q.
examples.note: Both the open door and the illuminated light are required.

limitations: Juxtaposition and multiplication signs are also used in Boolean algebra.

lookalikes.note: Conjunction requires both parts; inclusive disjunction requires at least one.

symbols.name: Definite description
symbols.summary: The individual satisfying P, when the governing description theory permits it.
symbols.body: The individual satisfying P, when the governing description theory permits it. Existence and uniqueness conditions vary by formal system. Whether a nonexisting or nonunique king yields a denotation depends on the adopted description theory.

examples.note: Whether a nonexisting or nonunique king yields a denotation depends on the adopted description theory.

limitations: Existence and uniqueness conditions vary by formal system.

symbols.name: Definition marker
symbols.summary: Introduces a definition or stipulated abbreviation.
symbols.body: Introduces a definition or stipulated abbreviation. A definition marker is not a claim of empirical identity. The right side stipulates the meaning of the abbreviation on the left.

examples.note: The right side stipulates the meaning of the abbreviation on the left.

limitations: A definition marker is not a claim of empirical identity.

symbols.name: Empty set
symbols.summary: The set with no elements.
symbols.body: The set with no elements. Not interchangeable with the falsity constant ⊥. There is no member of ∅ that could violate the subset condition.

examples.note: There is no member of ∅ that could violate the subset condition.

limitations: Not interchangeable with the falsity constant ⊥.

symbols.name: End-of-proof marker
symbols.summary: Marks the completion of a proof.
symbols.body: Marks the completion of a proof. □ also means necessity in modal logic. This is a document convention and adds no premise or inference.

examples.text: After deriving the required conclusion, write ∎.
examples.note: This is a document convention and adds no premise or inference.

limitations: □ also means necessity in modal logic.

symbols.name: Eventually operator
symbols.summary: φ holds at some relevant future time.
symbols.body: φ holds at some relevant future time. F can also denote prohibition or falsity in other contexts. At some relevant future state Delivered holds; no particular deadline is specified.

examples.note: At some relevant future state Delivered holds; no particular deadline is specified.

limitations: F can also denote prohibition or falsity in other contexts.

symbols.name: Exclusive disjunction
symbols.summary: Exactly one of p and q is true.
symbols.body: Exactly one of p and q is true. Definable as (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬(p ∧ q). Exactly one alternative is allowed; both true and both false are excluded.

examples.text: P means the coin lands heads; Q means it lands tails. P ⊕ Q.
examples.note: Exactly one alternative is allowed; both true and both false are excluded.

limitations: Definable as (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬(p ∧ q).

symbols.name: Existential quantifier
symbols.summary: There is at least one individual x for which P(x) holds.
symbols.body: There is at least one individual x for which P(x) holds. ∃ does not mean exactly one. At least one object is both a cat and black; other cats can have other colors.

examples.note: At least one object is both a cat and black; other cats can have other colors.

limitations: ∃ does not mean exactly one.

lookalikes.note: Existence requires at least one witness; unique existence additionally excludes distinct witnesses.

symbols.name: Failure of entailment
symbols.summary: At least one relevant interpretation satisfies Γ while falsifying φ.
symbols.body: At least one relevant interpretation satisfies Γ while falsifying φ. Does not entail Γ ⊨ ¬φ. P false and Q true provides a countermodel; the premise does not entail ¬P either.

examples.note: P false and Q true provides a countermodel; the premise does not entail ¬P either.

limitations: Does not entail Γ ⊨ ¬φ.

symbols.name: Falsity constant
symbols.summary: A formula that is always false.
symbols.body: A formula that is always false. Also used as the contradiction marker in natural deduction. The proof derives contradiction from a statement together with its negation.

examples.note: The proof derives contradiction from a statement together with its negation.

limitations: Also used as the contradiction marker in natural deduction.
Here arity 0 marks an atomic or schematic sign, not a truth-functional connective; its interpretation depends on its stated role.

lookalikes.note: Falsum is a logical constant; the empty set is a mathematical object.

symbols.name: Formal derivability
symbols.summary: φ has a formal derivation from Γ in the specified calculus.
symbols.body: φ has a formal derivation from Γ in the specified calculus. Always relative to a proof system. Modus ponens supplies a derivation in a proof system containing that rule.

examples.note: Modus ponens supplies a derivation in a proof system containing that rule.

limitations: Always relative to a proof system.

lookalikes.note: Provability is syntactic; entailment is semantic. Soundness and completeness connect them for suitable systems.

symbols.name: Formal nonderivability
symbols.summary: No derivation of φ from Γ exists in the specified calculus.
symbols.body: No derivation of φ from Γ exists in the specified calculus. Not synonymous with φ being false. Since a countermodel exists, soundness prevents such a derivation.

examples.text: P ∨ Q ⊬ P, in a sound classical proof system.
examples.note: Since a countermodel exists, soundness prevents such a derivation.

limitations: Not synonymous with φ being false.

symbols.name: Formula metavariable
symbols.summary: Ranges over formulas in a metalinguistic statement.
symbols.body: Ranges over formulas in a metalinguistic statement. Do not read φ as an individual variable unless the language explicitly assigns that role. φ is a placeholder for a formula, not a quantified individual inside the object language.

examples.text: For every formula φ, φ → φ is valid in classical logic.
examples.note: φ is a placeholder for a formula, not a quantified individual inside the object language.

limitations: Do not read φ as an individual variable unless the language explicitly assigns that role.
Here arity 0 marks an atomic or schematic sign, not a truth-functional connective; its interpretation depends on its stated role.

symbols.name: Function application
symbols.summary: A term denoting the function's output on the arguments.
symbols.body: A term denoting the function's output on the arguments. Terms denote objects; formulas express claims. MotherOf(a) is an object-denoting term; identity combines it with b to form a formula.

examples.note: MotherOf(a) is an object-denoting term; identity combines it with b to form a formula.

limitations: Terms denote objects; formulas express claims.
A predicate or function's actual arity is supplied by its signature. The integer here describes the displayed example, not every use of this notation.

symbols.name: Grouping delimiters
symbols.summary: Mark formula structure and operator scope.
symbols.body: Mark formula structure and operator scope. Braces often denote sets instead; punctuation depends on the language. The first denies their conjunction; the second requires Q and denies P.

examples.note: The first denies their conjunction; the second requires Q and denies P.

limitations: Braces often denote sets instead; punctuation depends on the language.
Here arity 0 marks an atomic or schematic sign, not a truth-functional connective; its interpretation depends on its stated role.

symbols.name: Hilbert choice operator
symbols.summary: Selects an object satisfying P when one exists, under an epsilon calculus.
symbols.body: Selects an object satisfying P when one exists, under an epsilon calculus. Not part of baseline first-order logic notation. The selected object supplies a witness when a witness exists.

examples.text: If ∃x P(x), then P(εx P(x)) in a suitable epsilon calculus.
examples.note: The selected object supplies a witness when a witness exists.

limitations: Not part of baseline first-order logic notation.

symbols.name: Identity
symbols.summary: The two terms denote the same individual.
symbols.body: The two terms denote the same individual. Identity is distinct from similarity, co-reference claims in opaque contexts, or logical equivalence. The two names denote one object, so the property transfers in this context.

examples.text: a = b; P(a). Therefore P(b), in an ordinary extensional first-order context.
examples.note: The two names denote one object, so the property transfers in this context.

limitations: Identity is distinct from similarity, co-reference claims in opaque contexts, or logical equivalence.

symbols.name: Inclusive disjunction
symbols.summary: At least one of p and q is true, possibly both.
symbols.body: At least one of p and q is true, possibly both. Computing uses | or || in some languages; | also denotes NAND elsewhere. The formula is true if Ada attends, Ben attends, or both attend.

examples.text: P means Ada attends; Q means Ben attends. P ∨ Q.
examples.note: The formula is true if Ada attends, Ben attends, or both attend.

limitations: Computing uses | or || in some languages; | also denotes NAND elsewhere.

lookalikes.note: Inclusive disjunction permits both operands to be true; exclusive disjunction does not.

symbols.name: Individual constant
symbols.summary: Denotes an individual under an interpretation.
symbols.body: Denotes an individual under an interpretation. A constant's interpretation can differ between structures. The name a denotes an individual; the formula applies Human to that individual.

examples.note: The name a denotes an individual; the formula applies Human to that individual.

limitations: A constant's interpretation can differ between structures.
Here arity 0 marks an atomic or schematic sign, not a truth-functional connective; its interpretation depends on its stated role.

symbols.name: Individual variable
symbols.summary: Ranges over individuals in the domain.
symbols.body: Ranges over individuals in the domain. These are variables, not quantifiers. x ranges over the domain and is bound by ∀; a remains an individual constant.

examples.note: x ranges over the domain and is bound by ∀; a remains an individual constant.

limitations: These are variables, not quantifiers.
Here arity 0 marks an atomic or schematic sign, not a truth-functional connective; its interpretation depends on its stated role.

symbols.name: Interpretation brackets
symbols.summary: Denotes a semantic value under a stated interpretation.
symbols.body: Denotes a semantic value under a stated interpretation. The value can be a truth value, extension, intension, or other semantic object. The brackets refer to the formula's semantic value rather than merely its written form.

examples.text: ⟦P ∧ Q⟧ᵥ = true when valuation v makes both P and Q true.
examples.note: The brackets refer to the formula's semantic value rather than merely its written form.

limitations: The value can be a truth value, extension, intension, or other semantic object.

symbols.name: Knowledge operator
symbols.summary: Agent a knows φ in the specified epistemic system.
symbols.body: Agent a knows φ in the specified epistemic system. The adopted axioms determine the modeled idealizations about knowledge. In a standard epistemic model, P holds throughout the worlds compatible with agent a's knowledge.

examples.note: In a standard epistemic model, P holds throughout the worlds compatible with agent a's knowledge.

limitations: The adopted axioms determine the modeled idealizations about knowledge.

symbols.name: Lambda abstraction
symbols.summary: Forms a function or abstraction from a variable and an expression.
symbols.body: Forms a function or abstraction from a variable and an expression. Not a connective of ordinary first-order logic. The bound variable is replaced by the argument according to the calculus's reduction rules.

examples.note: The bound variable is replaced by the argument according to the calculus's reduction rules.

limitations: Not a connective of ordinary first-order logic.

symbols.name: Logical equivalence marker
symbols.summary: The formulas agree in truth across the relevant interpretations.
symbols.body: The formulas agree in truth across the relevant interpretations. Notation varies; some authors use these signs inside the object language instead. De Morgan's law states that both formulas agree on every valuation.

examples.note: De Morgan's law states that both formulas agree on every valuation.

limitations: Notation varies; some authors use these signs inside the object language instead.

symbols.name: Logical validity marker
symbols.summary: φ holds in every relevant interpretation.
symbols.body: φ holds in every relevant interpretation. For propositional logic, a tautology; semantic classes can differ in other logics. Every classical valuation makes this formula true; other logics require separate assessment.

examples.note: Every classical valuation makes this formula true; other logics require separate assessment.

limitations: For propositional logic, a tautology; semantic classes can differ in other logics.

symbols.name: Material biconditional
symbols.summary: p if and only if q: they have the same truth value.
symbols.body: p if and only if q: they have the same truth value. ≡ and ⇔ may instead denote metalinguistic equivalence; check the convention. Both directions are asserted, so either truth-value mismatch makes the formula false.

examples.text: P means the number is even; Q means it is divisible by two. P ↔ Q.
examples.note: Both directions are asserted, so either truth-value mismatch makes the formula false.

limitations: ≡ and ⇔ may instead denote metalinguistic equivalence; check the convention.

lookalikes.note: The biconditional requires both directions; the conditional requires only one.

symbols.name: Material conditional
symbols.summary: If p then q; false exactly when p is true and q is false.
symbols.body: If p then q; false exactly when p is true and q is false. Does not by itself assert causation or relevance. ⇒ is also used by some authors. A counterexample is an on switch with an unlit lamp. The formula alone gives no causal mechanism.

examples.text: P means the switch is on; Q means the lamp is lit. P → Q.
examples.note: A counterexample is an on switch with an unlit lamp. The formula alone gives no causal mechanism.

limitations: Does not by itself assert causation or relevance. ⇒ is also used by some authors.
In English, 'P only if Q' places P in the antecedent and Q in the consequent; 'P if Q' reverses those roles.

lookalikes.note: A conditional is a formula; semantic consequence relates premises to conclusions over interpretations.
Treating the conditional as reversible produces this formal fallacy.

symbols.name: Model satisfaction
symbols.summary: φ is satisfied in structure M under assignment s.
symbols.body: φ is satisfied in structure M under assignment s. The same glyph is used in related but distinct semantic roles. In the particular structure M, a denotes an object in the extension of Cat.

examples.note: In the particular structure M, a denotes an object in the extension of Cat.

limitations: The same glyph is used in related but distinct semantic roles.

symbols.name: NAND
symbols.summary: Not both p and q.
symbols.body: Not both p and q. The stroke | has unrelated uses in other systems. The formula fails only when both alarms are active.

examples.text: P means alarm A is active; Q means alarm B is active. P ↑ Q.
examples.note: The formula fails only when both alarms are active.

limitations: The stroke | has unrelated uses in other systems.

symbols.name: Necessity operator
symbols.summary: φ is necessary under the chosen modal semantics.
symbols.body: φ is necessary under the chosen modal semantics. An extension beyond ordinary propositional and first-order logic. P holds at every world accessible from the current world in the chosen modal model.

examples.note: P holds at every world accessible from the current world in the chosen modal model.

limitations: An extension beyond ordinary propositional and first-order logic.

lookalikes.note: Necessity concerns every accessible world; possibility requires at least one.

symbols.name: Negated existential quantifier
symbols.summary: No individual in the domain satisfies P.
symbols.body: No individual in the domain satisfies P. An abbreviation for a negated existential formula. Nothing in the domain is both a cat and a reptile.

examples.note: Nothing in the domain is both a cat and a reptile.

limitations: An abbreviation for a negated existential formula.

symbols.name: Negation
englishReadings: it is not the case that
symbols.summary: Not p: reverses its truth value.
symbols.body: Not p: reverses its truth value. ! is common in computing; N is Polish prefix notation. The formula says the door is not open; it does not say the door is locked.

examples.text: P means the door is open. ¬P.
examples.note: The formula says the door is not open; it does not say the door is locked.

limitations: ! is common in computing; N is Polish prefix notation.

lookalikes.note: Negating a conjunction differs from negating each conjunct and retaining conjunction.
Contradiction is the concept of incompatible truth commitments; ¬ is a formal connective.

symbols.name: Next operator
symbols.summary: φ holds at the next state.
symbols.body: φ holds at the next state. Typically used with a discrete successor-time semantics. Ready must hold at the next state, rather than merely at some later state.

examples.note: Ready must hold at the next state, rather than merely at some later state.

limitations: Typically used with a discrete successor-time semantics.

symbols.name: Nonidentity
symbols.summary: The terms denote different individuals.
symbols.body: The terms denote different individuals. Usually defined using negation and identity. The interpretation must assign the two terms different objects.

examples.note: The interpretation must assign the two terms different objects.

limitations: Usually defined using negation and identity.

symbols.name: NOR
symbols.summary: Neither p nor q.
symbols.body: Neither p nor q. Definable as ¬(p ∨ q). The formula holds only when neither person is present.

examples.text: P means Ada is present; Q means Ben is present. P ↓ Q.
examples.note: The formula holds only when neither person is present.

limitations: Definable as ¬(p ∨ q).

symbols.name: Obligation operator
symbols.summary: φ is obligatory under the chosen deontic interpretation.
symbols.body: φ is obligatory under the chosen deontic interpretation. Conditional obligations need richer notation or semantics. The formula represents an obligation; it does not assert that the book is actually returned.

examples.note: The formula represents an obligation; it does not assert that the book is actually returned.

limitations: Conditional obligations need richer notation or semantics.

symbols.name: Permission operator
symbols.summary: φ is permitted under the chosen deontic interpretation.
symbols.body: φ is permitted under the chosen deontic interpretation. P is also a predicate letter elsewhere; context is essential. The action is permitted in the modeled normative system, without being required.

examples.note: The action is permitted in the modeled normative system, without being required.

limitations: P is also a predicate letter elsewhere; context is essential.

symbols.name: Possibility operator
symbols.summary: φ is possible under the chosen modal semantics.
symbols.body: φ is possible under the chosen modal semantics. In standard normal modal logics, ◇φ abbreviates ¬□¬φ. At least one accessible world satisfies P in the standard Kripke interpretation.

examples.note: At least one accessible world satisfies P in the standard Kripke interpretation.

limitations: In standard normal modal logics, ◇φ abbreviates ¬□¬φ.

symbols.name: Predicate application
symbols.summary: Asserts that the object denoted by a satisfies P.
symbols.body: Asserts that the object denoted by a satisfies P. Some notations omit parentheses. The formula says that the individual denoted by ada belongs to the extension of Tall.

examples.note: The formula says that the individual denoted by ada belongs to the extension of Tall.

limitations: Some notations omit parentheses.

symbols.name: Predicate letter
symbols.summary: Denotes a property or relation of a specified arity.
symbols.body: Denotes a property or relation of a specified arity. Arity must be declared; a unary predicate and binary relation are different uses. P applies to one term and R to two; the symbolization key supplies their intended meanings.

examples.text: P is unary; R is binary. P(a) ∧ R(a, b).
examples.note: P applies to one term and R to two; the symbolization key supplies their intended meanings.

limitations: Arity must be declared; a unary predicate and binary relation are different uses.
Here arity 0 marks an atomic or schematic sign, not a truth-functional connective; its interpretation depends on its stated role.
A predicate or function's actual arity is supplied by its signature. The integer here describes the displayed example, not every use of this notation.

symbols.name: Premise-set metavariable
symbols.summary: Represents a set, list, or multiset of premises, depending on the calculus.
symbols.body: Represents a set, list, or multiset of premises, depending on the calculus. Structural rules depend on whether order and multiplicity matter. Γ abbreviates the premises and is not an additional premise letter.

examples.note: Γ abbreviates the premises and is not an additional premise letter.

limitations: Structural rules depend on whether order and multiplicity matter.
Here arity 0 marks an atomic or schematic sign, not a truth-functional connective; its interpretation depends on its stated role.

symbols.name: Prohibition operator
symbols.summary: φ is forbidden under the chosen deontic interpretation.
symbols.body: φ is forbidden under the chosen deontic interpretation. Commonly defined as O¬φ; F also means eventually in temporal logic. Under the common definition O¬φ, refraining from indoor smoking is obligatory.

examples.note: Under the common definition O¬φ, refraining from indoor smoking is obligatory.

limitations: Commonly defined as O¬φ; F also means eventually in temporal logic.

symbols.name: Proper subset
symbols.summary: A is a subset of B and A differs from B.
symbols.body: A is a subset of B and A differs from B. Some authors use ⊂ for this meaning. Inclusion holds and the larger set has an element, 3, absent from the smaller one.

examples.note: Inclusion holds and the larger set has an element, 3, absent from the smaller one.

limitations: Some authors use ⊂ for this meaning.

symbols.name: Relation application
symbols.summary: Asserts that a and b stand in relation R in that order.
symbols.body: Asserts that a and b stand in relation R in that order. A relation need not be symmetric. The order matters: Ada being taller than Ben does not imply the reverse.

examples.note: The order matters: Ada being taller than Ben does not imply the reverse.

limitations: A relation need not be symmetric.

symbols.name: Semantic consequence
symbols.summary: Every relevant interpretation satisfying Γ also satisfies φ.
symbols.body: Every relevant interpretation satisfying Γ also satisfies φ. Semantic consequence is not the material conditional → or syntactic derivability ⊢. No valuation makes both premises true while making Q false.

examples.note: No valuation makes both premises true while making Q false.

limitations: Semantic consequence is not the material conditional → or syntactic derivability ⊢.

lookalikes.note: Semantic consequence concerns models; derivability concerns proofs in a calculus.

symbols.name: Sentence letter
symbols.summary: Represents an atomic proposition under a chosen valuation.
symbols.body: Represents an atomic proposition under a chosen valuation. Letters have no fixed subject matter and are distinct from formula metavariables. p names the proposition for this formalization; it is not a variable ranging over trains.

examples.text: Assign p the sentence 'the train is late'.
examples.note: p names the proposition for this formalization; it is not a variable ranging over trains.

limitations: Letters have no fixed subject matter and are distinct from formula metavariables.
Here arity 0 marks an atomic or schematic sign, not a truth-functional connective; its interpretation depends on its stated role.

symbols.name: Sequent arrow
symbols.summary: Separates antecedent and succedent in a sequent calculus.
symbols.body: Separates antecedent and succedent in a sequent calculus. May have different interpretations in classical, intuitionistic, and substructural calculi. The antecedent contains the two premises and the succedent contains the conclusion.

examples.note: The antecedent contains the two premises and the succedent contains the conclusion.

limitations: May have different interpretations in classical, intuitionistic, and substructural calculi.

symbols.name: Set intersection
symbols.summary: The set containing objects in both A and B.
symbols.body: The set containing objects in both A and B. Related to conjunction but is a set operation, not a propositional connective. Only 2 belongs to both input sets.

examples.note: Only 2 belongs to both input sets.

limitations: Related to conjunction but is a set operation, not a propositional connective.

symbols.name: Set membership
symbols.summary: Object x belongs to set A.
symbols.body: Object x belongs to set A. This is a nonlogical predicate of ordinary set-theoretic languages, not a universal FOL primitive. The numeral 2 denotes an element of the displayed set.

examples.note: The numeral 2 denotes an element of the displayed set.

limitations: This is a nonlogical predicate of ordinary set-theoretic languages, not a universal FOL primitive.

lookalikes.note: Membership relates an object to a set; inclusion relates sets through their members.

symbols.name: Set nonmembership
symbols.summary: Object x does not belong to set A.
symbols.body: Object x does not belong to set A. Abbreviates negated membership. The displayed set contains no element equal to 4.

examples.note: The displayed set contains no element equal to 4.

limitations: Abbreviates negated membership.

symbols.name: Set union
symbols.summary: The set containing objects in A or B.
symbols.body: The set containing objects in A or B. Related to disjunction but is a set operation, not a propositional connective. An object from either input belongs to the union; repetitions do not create additional elements.

examples.note: An object from either input belongs to the union; repetitions do not create additional elements.

limitations: Related to disjunction but is a set operation, not a propositional connective.

symbols.name: Subset
symbols.summary: Every member of A is a member of B.
symbols.body: Every member of A is a member of B. ⊂ is ambiguous between strict and non-strict inclusion across authors. Every element of the first set belongs to the second.

examples.note: Every element of the first set belongs to the second.

limitations: ⊂ is ambiguous between strict and non-strict inclusion across authors.

symbols.name: Substitution notation
symbols.summary: Replace free occurrences of x in φ by t subject to capture restrictions.
symbols.body: Replace free occurrences of x in φ by t subject to capture restrictions. Some authors reverse the order inside the brackets; declare the convention. Replace the free x by a. Substituting a variable may require renaming binders to avoid capture.

examples.note: Replace the free x by a. Substituting a variable may require renaming binders to avoid capture.

limitations: Some authors reverse the order inside the brackets; declare the convention.

symbols.name: Theoremhood marker
symbols.summary: φ can be derived with no undischarged premises.
symbols.body: φ can be derived with no undischarged premises. A theorem of the specified calculus. The conditional can be proved without any undischarged assumption.

examples.note: The conditional can be proved without any undischarged assumption.

limitations: A theorem of the specified calculus.

symbols.name: Therefore marker
symbols.summary: Introduces an argument's conclusion.
symbols.body: Introduces an argument's conclusion. The mark does not certify that the argument is valid. The marker identifies the conclusion; validity still depends on the premises and inference.

examples.note: The marker identifies the conclusion; validity still depends on the premises and inference.

limitations: The mark does not certify that the argument is valid.

symbols.name: Truth constant
symbols.summary: A formula that is always true.
symbols.body: A formula that is always true. T can also be a sentence letter; 1 is a Boolean-algebra convention. This has the same truth value as P because the right conjunct is always true.

examples.note: This has the same truth value as P because the right conjunct is always true.

limitations: T can also be a sentence letter; 1 is a Boolean-algebra convention.
Here arity 0 marks an atomic or schematic sign, not a truth-functional connective; its interpretation depends on its stated role.

lookalikes.note: ⊤ is an object-language truth constant; ⊨ asserts semantic validity in the metalanguage.

symbols.name: Type annotation
symbols.summary: Term t has type τ in the relevant context.
symbols.body: Term t has type τ in the relevant context. A colon also has ordinary punctuation and set-builder uses. The context assigns x the Boolean type, restricting its admissible use in typed expressions.

examples.note: The context assigns x the Boolean type, restricting its admissible use in typed expressions.

limitations: A colon also has ordinary punctuation and set-builder uses.

symbols.name: Unique existential quantifier
symbols.summary: Exactly one individual satisfies P.
symbols.body: Exactly one individual satisfies P. Usually a defined abbreviation, not a primitive of first-order logic. There is a captain, and any two objects satisfying Captain must be identical.

examples.note: There is a captain, and any two objects satisfying Captain must be identical.

limitations: Usually a defined abbreviation, not a primitive of first-order logic.

symbols.name: Universal quantifier
symbols.summary: For every individual x in the domain, P(x) holds.
symbols.body: For every individual x in the domain, P(x) holds. Universal quantification does not imply that P has an instance in every logic or domain convention. Every object that is a cat is a mammal. The formula does not assert that cats exist.

examples.note: Every object that is a cat is a mammal. The formula does not assert that cats exist.

limitations: Classical first-order semantics normally assumes a nonempty domain. In systems permitting empty domains, universal formulas are vacuously true there.
Even in a nonempty domain, ∀x(Unicorn(x) → Blue(x)) does not assert that any unicorn exists.
The bound variable need not occur in the body: ∀x P is syntactically permitted in many systems and is vacuous quantification.

lookalikes.note: Universal quantification requires the property throughout the domain; existential quantification requires a witness.

symbols.name: Until operator
symbols.summary: ψ eventually holds and φ holds at preceding relevant times.
symbols.body: ψ eventually holds and φ holds at preceding relevant times. Weak until is a distinct operator and need not guarantee ψ. Service eventually occurs, and Waiting holds at each preceding relevant state.

examples.note: Service eventually occurs, and Waiting holds at each preceding relevant state.

limitations: Weak until is a distinct operator and need not guarantee ψ.
